meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Not all those who wander are lost'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine J.R.R. Tolkien — the second line of the Aragorn poem in The Fellowship of the Ring (1954), commonly misquoted as 'Not all who wander are lost.'

answer.label: Written by
answer.authorDates: 1892–1973 · English writer, poet & philologist; author of The Lord of the Rings
answer.sourceLine: This is the second line of Tolkien’s poem “The Riddle of Strider” — known by its first line, “All that is gold does not glitter” — in The Fellowship of the Ring (1954). It appears in Gandalf’s letter to Frodo, read in the chapter “Strider,” and describes the wandering ranger Aragorn as the hidden heir of kings. The exact wording is confirmed verbatim in the text.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: “The Riddle of Strider” (a.k.a. “All that is gold does not glitter”)
Book I, chapter “Strider” — in Gandalf’s letter to Frodo

source.excerpt:
All that is gold does not glitter,
Not all those who wander are lost;
The old that is strong does not wither,
Deep roots are not reached by the frost.

From the ashes a fire shall be woken,
A light from the shadows shall spring;
Renewed shall be blade that was broken,
The crownless again shall be king.
trail: Tolkien’s dedicated Wikipedia entry for the phrase traces it to “the second line of J. R. R. Tolkien’s poem ‘The Riddle of Strider’ from The Fellowship of the Ring, 1954.”
Wikiquote’s sourced entry places the poem in the chapter “Strider,” where it introduces Aragorn.
The full poem as reproduced from the novel reads “Not all those who wander are lost” — with the word “those” the popular version routinely drops.
source.excerptNote: The full eight-line poem. The famous line is the second, and in the story it is a riddle confirming that the road-worn ranger Strider is really Aragorn, the rightful king.
source.rightsHolder: The J.R.R. Tolkien Estate and its publishers (HarperCollins; Houghton Mifflin Harcourt)
source.rightsNote: The Fellowship of the Ring was first published in 1954, so under current U.S. law this text remains in copyright. Tolkien died in 1973, and The Lord of the Rings is controlled by the Tolkien Estate and its publishers — the poem is not public domain.

author.bio: John Ronald Reuel Tolkien (1892–1973) was an English writer, poet and Oxford philologist, best known for The Hobbit and The Lord of the Rings. A professor of Anglo-Saxon and English language, he built Middle-earth partly to give his invented languages a world to live in. The Aragorn poem containing this line first appeared in The Fellowship of the Ring in 1954.

misattribution.heading: The catch
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right — this really is Tolkien. What goes wrong is the wording and the context.

items.who: Countless tattoos, mugs and travel captions
items.why: Tolkien wrote “Not all those who wander are lost.” The hugely popular shortened form — “Not all who wander are lost” — quietly drops the word “those,” as the record of the line shows.

It is usually read as a free-spirited motto about travel. In the book it is a riddle identifying the ranger Aragorn as the hidden heir to the throne — “one of the lines from Tolkien’s work most often quoted out of context.”

misattribution.truthLine: The line is authentic Tolkien — the second line of the Aragorn poem in The Fellowship of the Ring (1954) — and the only common error is dropping the word “those.”

context.heading: Why it endures
lead: In the story the verse is not about travel at all: it is a test. Gandalf leaves it in a letter so Frodo can recognise the mysterious, weather-worn stranger “Strider” at Bree as Aragorn — the crownless heir who will again be king. The wanderer only looks lost.
That gap between the book’s meaning and the modern one is exactly why the line travels so well: stripped of Middle-earth, it reads as reassurance that aimlessness can be purpose in disguise.
